assessmentSummary.identity: A side-on, side-specific two-hand medicine-ball wall throw using a declared rotational countermovement, ground-up hip-pelvis-trunk sequence, transverse release, controlled finish, and full reset.
currentCardFindings: The legacy card already declares rotational projection, hip and thoracic rotation, shoulder horizontal action, and ground-up force transfer.
It lacks exact stance, pivot, ball start, wall target, return, side, dose, and difficulty dimensions.
Its transverse projection is a deterministic boundary from the generic card's forward chest action.
Five candidates have healthy oEmbed metadata only; no human media approval is created.

currentCardSnapshot.description: Stand side-on to an inspected wall with one exact medicine ball and a declared throwing side. Use the declared fixed-stance or pivot-allowed rotational countermovement, sequence force from feet through hips, pelvis, trunk, shoulders, arms, and ball, release transversely to the declared wall target, finish under control, wait for the return path, retrieve without crossing an active lane, and fully reset.

population.selectionBoundary: Select exact ball, mass, side, stance, pivot, preload, target, contacts, attempts, rest, and return policy from current readiness; exercise cards do not carry skill levels.

evidence.sourceTitle: Land-Based Strength and Conditioning for Swimming
claims: A standing rotational wall toss uses side-on orientation and ground-up transverse force transfer.
The explicit identity is a side-specific countermovement rotational medicine-ball throw, distinct from forward bilateral chest projection.

evidence.sourceTitle: Land-Based Strength and Conditioning for Swimming
claims: Medicine-ball throws require exact stance, countermovement, projection, target, release, contacts, and reset taxonomy.
Declare forward versus transverse projection and bilateral versus side-specific sequencing.

evidence.sourceTitle: Influence of trunk rotator strength on rotational medicine ball throwing performance
evidence.sourcePublisher: Journal of Sports Medicine and Physical Fitness
claims: Rotational throwing performance relates to trunk rotator strength, while full-body throws also use lower-body drive and upper-limb release.
Declare foot, ankle, knee, hip, pelvis, spine, scapulothoracic, shoulder, elbow, wrist and hand roles.

evidence.sourceTitle: Factorial Structure of Motor Abilities and Skills in Different Age Groups of Elite Female Soccer Players
evidence.sourcePublisher: International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health
claims: Dynamic medicine-ball throws use a declared countermovement to create momentum before release.
Observe ball start, lower-body preload, ground-up sequence, trunk control, projection plane, release, foot contacts, finish, and reset.

evidence.sourceTitle: Reliability of seated and standing throwing velocity using differently weighted medicine balls
evidence.sourcePublisher: Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research
claims: Ball load and standing protocol affect measured throwing velocity.
Score exact variants on exercise complexity and physical difficulty and derive overall difficulty as their maximum; no exercise skill level is assigned.

evidence.sourceTitle: Validation of a Supine Upper-Body Power Test in Physically Active Male and Female Adults Using a Medicine Ball With Accelerometer
evidence.sourcePublisher: Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research
claims: Medicine-ball output can be quantified and declines when effort or technique changes.
Track ball mass, high-intent throws, output loss, shoulder and elbow response, trunk control, contact or catch load, and recovery.

evidence.sourceTitle: Medicine Ball Lunge to Chest Pass
claims: ACE requires a prepared partner or suitable wall or rebounder, target distance, stable stance, and clear intent.
Declare ball type and mass, wall or partner behavior, target, release lane, return and catch policy, traction, clearance, traffic, retrieval, and coach sightline.
Explosive medicine-ball work should preserve power rather than become fatigue conditioning.
Use short sets, full reset, and enough rest to preserve ball speed, projection, target accuracy, posture, contacts, and safe retrieval.

evidence.sourceTitle: Med Ball Chest Throw Against Wall
evidence.sourcePublisher: U.S. Marine Corps Training and Education Command
claims: The U.S. Marine Corps demonstration identifies a medicine-ball chest throw against a wall as an upper-body power task.
Instructions must name exact stance, ball start, countermovement, projection, target, foot contacts, release, return or retrieval, reset, and stop signal.

evidence.sourceTitle: Medicine Ball Lunge to Chest Pass
claims: Partner and wall throws require target readiness and force-aware catching.
Stop for pain or neurologic symptoms, loss of balance, spinal compensation, mistimed release, unsafe foot contacts, damaged ball, occupied lane, unsafe rebound or partner, or output loss.

evidence.sourceTitle: Criterion Validity and Reliability of a New Medicine Ball Rotational Power Test
evidence.sourcePublisher: Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research
claims: Medicine-ball throws can serve as standardized power tasks when protocol is controlled.
Use early and fresh for power expression; hold mass and variant constant for comparison and do not use maximal throws as conditioning filler.

evidence.sourceTitle: Medicine Ball Lunge to Chest Pass
claims: Athlete support should show direction, target, ball specification, contacts, cue, reset, and stop signal.
Offer a lighter or softer ball, smaller countermovement, lower-intent rehearsal, fewer attempts, longer rest, high-contrast target, and nonvideo instruction.

evidence.sourceTitle: Criterion Validity and Reliability of a New Medicine Ball Rotational Power Test
evidence.sourcePublisher: Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research
claims: Reliable power testing requires a standardized throw protocol.
Expose projection, side, ball mass, target, contacts, attempt count, rest, output measure, observation angle, invalid-attempt rule, return control, and lane shutdown.

evidence.sourceTitle: Medicine Ball Lunge to Chest Pass
claims: Wall or trained-partner targets can provide a visible forward target when logistics permit.
Offer lighter or softer balls, smaller preload, no jump, shorter range, fewer repetitions, longer reset, high-contrast target, plain text, and an appropriate nonthrow substitute.

evidence.sourceTitle: Factorial Structure of Motor Abilities and Skills in Different Age Groups of Elite Female Soccer Players
evidence.sourcePublisher: International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health
claims: Projection direction and release path define separate throw tasks.
Ball mass, exact distance, and measurement are annotations; rotation, overhead, scoop, slam, vertical, chest, and backward projections require explicit identity review.
